transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-25
Start time (UTC): 14:00
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions), Liam Zhou (MeridianFlow CTO), Marta Ruiz (Head of Platform), Evan Cho (Eng Manager), Sana Patel (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
- Intro + partner fit discussion; MeridianFlow is evaluating hybrid edge GPU routing for real-time inference across regional PoPs.
- Key constraints: tenancy isolation, burst GPU capacity, VPC/on-prem enclave for regulated clients, and approval process for audit logging.
- Agreed next steps: exchange perf traces, share integration checklist, schedule SE deep-dive, draft pilot SOW.

Topics: partner integration, dedicated vs hosted routing, KV cache / prefix caching, VPC peering / on-prem envelopes, SOC2 and KMS, cost/levers (batching/quantization).

Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on this team. Quick intros, we'll pass to Priya for the tech overview but first maybe Liam, can you give a 60-second on MeridianFlow and why you're talking to partners like us?
[00:18] Liam: Sure, yeah thanks. So MeridianFlow we run an edge mesh, kind of a CDN for inference, targeting retail and telco use cases. We're seeing a lot more demand for low-latency chat and personalized recommender inference on the edge, and we need partners that can help with GPU routing and model serving, so minimal warmup time, predictable tail latency.
[00:38] Marta: And to add, a few of our customers are regulated so we sometimes need private enclaves or on-prem options. That's a big part of the evaluation.
[00:45] Alex: Got it. Priya, you wanna give a quick picture of how Redwood would fit here?
[00:49] Priya: Yeah, hi all. Priya from Redwood infra team. At a high level, we do three deployment modes; hosted API for quick go-to, dedicated GPU pools for committed capacity, and private VPC/on-prem packs for regulated customers, so sounds like some mix that might map to your PoPs. We optimize routing, batching, and caching — prefix/KV caching is a big win for repeated prompts.
[01:10] Evan: When you say KV caching, do you mean you keep kv cache at the serving layer on the GPU nodes or do you offload to a sidecar? I ask because our edge nodes are disk-constrained.
[01:20] Priya: Good question. We generally keep KV cache in GPU memory for hot prefixes, but there's a tiered approach: hot in-GPU, warm in local RAM, and cold in a small fast sidecar store. We can tune retention per-customer. Sidecar could be an in-memory LRU store, not always required. Sorry, I said k-v cash earlier — transcription is —
[01:39] Jordan: (laughs) k-v cash — we wish it paid us.
[01:42] Liam: One of the things we need is tenancy isolation across different enterprise customers. Some require dedicated pools per customer. What's the smallest footprint for a dedicated pool?
[01:53] Priya: We can do per-customer dedicated pools starting at an N GPU commit, depends on model family and sequence lengths. For quantized models we can fit more per GPU. We usually recommend a proof-of-concept with a small dedicated pool and autoscale/burst for spikes. Pricing bands vary. Alex will follow up with ranges.
[02:12] Alex: Quick clarifying: do you have preferred GPU types across your PoPs? A100, H100, or smaller A30-ish?
[02:22] Marta: We have mixed hardware. A couple of PoPs have H100, a few older ones have A100s, and for some telco partners we use Ampere-based small instances — lower mem. We wanted to understand what your runtime supports and how you pick kernels.
[02:35] Priya: We have a kernel-selection layer that picks the best execution path by model architecture, seq len, and hw. For lower-memory GPUs we use quantized execution and smaller batch sizes. There are tradeoffs of latency vs throughput.
[02:48] Evan: Latency is our main SLO — 95th p99 not exceed 120ms for single-turn chat across PoPs. Cost is secondary but important. Can Redwood meet that with a hybrid approach?
[02:58] Priya: Yes, with routing by latency SLO and prefix caching we can drop tail substantially. We may route short-turn requests to smaller quantized variants and fallback to full models for heavy payloads — automatic fallback is supported.
[03:12] Sana: From security perspective, we need to see SOC2, network diagrams, and we'd prefer a customer-managed KMS for keying. Do you support HSM or BYOK?
[03:23] Priya: We integrate with customer KMS for private deployments; HSM works in the private plane for on-prem as well. For hosted we offer envelope encryption and can support BYOK for enterprise tiers. We'll share the security pack.
[03:35] Liam: What's the onboarding timeline for a pilot? Our procurement window is roughly 6–8 weeks, and we want a pilot in 2 months if possible.
[03:43] Alex: That sounds doable; typical timeline is discovery -> SOW -> pilot with 4–6 week pilot. We'll try to compress if you can provide traces and acceptance criteria.
[03:51] Marta: About routing — we need region-aware routing that can failover to nearest region during outages and still enforce data residency for some customers. Can Redwood do per-customer routing policies?
[04:05] Priya: Yes, routing policies are policy driven; you can pin by region, cost tier, or latency. We also support automatic fallback to compatible model variants in another region if capacity is constrained. Data residency flags can be attached to requests and enforced in the control plane.
[04:22] Evan: Two technical constraints to call out: first, we have a burst pattern from retail — short spikes where we need 10x baseline for minutes. Second, we need model version pinning per customer to avoid regressions. How do you handle burst capacity?
[04:36] Priya: Autoscale + burst pools handle short spikes, but for predictable peaks we recommend reserved capacity. We also have an automatic fallback policy: if reserved is exhausted, route to cheaper variants or lower-precision models. Version pinning is supported in the deployment abstraction.
[04:48] Jordan: I'll add, we can also do canary rollouts and A/B via the Console so you can compare quality and cost simultaneously.
[04:56] Liam: How intrusive is the integration? We run a fairly lightweight control plane at the edge, we don't want heavy new agents.
[05:02] Alex: Good point — Priya can describe minimal integration hooks.
[05:06] Priya: Integration is usually an API endpoint plus a small sidecar for caching and metrics. Sidecar is optional if you already have a fast local cache. For private/on-prem we ship a small bundle that talks back to the control plane over an outbound connection — no inbound firewall holes required usually.
[05:20] Evan: Are there examples of customers who run similar mixed-hardware PoP fleets with Redwood?
[05:26] Priya: We have a few telco and retail partners running variants; I won't name names on the call but we'll share anonymized patterns in the checklist doc.
[05:34] Sana: About audit logs — we need request-level audit for specific enterprise clients for at least 180 days, retained off the GPU nodes. Can you guarantee that?
[05:45] Priya: Yes, logs are streamed to a separate observability backend and can be exported to your S3 or syslog. Retention is configurable based on plan. For Private we can ensure logs never leave your VPC unless you opt in.
[05:58] Liam: One friction point: our procurement hates vendor lock-in. Is there a clear exit path and standard artifacts to hand back?
[06:07] Alex: We provide model and config export, KV snapshots, and a migration playbook. We'll include an exit appendix in the SOW.
[06:15] Marta: Pricing — rough bands fine. We need a sense of cost per token or per-hour per GPU for dedicated pools to model economics.
[06:24] Alex: We'll send ranges after the call. For pilots we can offer credits; for committed it's a monthly banding with volume tiers.
[06:31] Evan: One last infra question — what network patterns do you require? VPC peering, private link, or just public egress with mTLS?
[06:40] Priya: Many customers prefer PrivateLink or VPC peering for lower latency. We support VPC peering, PrivateLink, and TLS with mTLS for hosted API. For on-prem we use outbound-only control plane connections.
[06:51] Jordan: Also worth noting token-level cost can change significantly with batching and prefix caching; we'll show you sample tradeoff curves in follow-up.
[07:00] Liam: Ok, would be good to see an architecture sketch of how Redwood would sit between our edge orchestrator and the GPUs.
[07:06] Alex: We'll include a lightweight architecture diagram.
[07:09] (30s silence while doc links are pasted)
[07:42] Marta: On compliance, a couple quick things — we need SSO/SAML integration, RBAC, and also region-based role separation.
[07:52] Priya: SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported; Console offers role scoping and token scoping. Region-based separation is modeled by tagging resources.
[08:00] Evan: For the pilot acceptance criteria, our main metric is p95 latency under production-like traffic and no more than 2% degradation in quality relative to our baseline model. Can we tie quality checks to the same prompt set?
[08:13] Priya: Definitely — we integrate evals and can run regression alerts tied to your prompt sets. We'll include the quality monitoring flow in the checklist.
[08:22] Sana: Data residency question again: some customers want complete data non-retention for 30 days. Is that supported per-customer?
[08:31] Priya: Yes per-customer retention policies are configurable; Private is easiest for strict non-retention.
[08:36] Liam: Can we do a small smoke pilot next month? We have sample traffic and a sandbox PoP.
[08:43] Alex: That's the plan. We'll draft an SOW and run a bandwidth/throughput baseline next.
[08:48] Evan: Also, we may want to try quantized LLM variants for cost. Any constraints on model family?
[08:55] Priya: We support most open model families and have profiles for quantization; some very recent arch tweaks might need additional vetting but in general we support Llama-derived, Mistral-ish, and other common families. (transcription: Mistral sometimes shows as mister-all)
[09:12] Marta: Who will be our primary tech contact at Redwood for the deep dive?
[09:16] Alex: Priya will lead SE work, Jordan will support architecture and pilot config, and I'll shepherd the commercial.
[09:22] (short cross-talk)
[09:26] Priya: For the technical deep dive we'll want: request/response size distribution, token lengths, typical concurrency, and any specific L7 routing you have. Evan, can you send that?
[09:35] Evan: Yep, I'll pull 7 days and send. Expect it by early next week.
[09:39] (background: someone typing)
[09:46] Sana: We'll need the SOC2 docs before security can sign off on the pilot; send over a secure link if possible.
[09:53] Alex: Absolutely. I'll drop the pack to the secure share.
[09:57] Liam: Two small product asks: 1) per-customer cost reporting per token, and 2) a way to route only a % of traffic to a new model variant for canary. You mentioned A/B — is % routing supported?
[10:08] Jordan: Yes, percent-based routing is supported in the Console; cost reporting per token is in the Optimize tool — we can enable token-level breakdowns for your pilot.
[10:17] Evan: One potential blocker — some of our PoPs run older drivers, and we've seen kernel incompatibility with some inference runtimes. Do you have a compatibility matrix?
[10:26] Priya: We do and we'll share it. For older drivers we often use CPU fallbacks or smaller model variants as stopgaps, but ideally we update drivers.
[10:34] Alex: Ok, let's summarize actions and owners.
[10:37] Alex: Priya will send the integration checklist and compatibility matrix. Evan will send 7-day traffic distribution. Sana will specify compliance must-haves. I'll send SOW + pricing bands and SOC2 links. We'll schedule deep dive week of Feb 6.
[10:50] Liam: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:52] Marta: No, that's all. Thanks everyone.
[10:55] Alex: Thanks all, talk soon.

Call end remarks / recap (auto):
- Partner fit: strong overlap; MeridianFlow needs hybrid routing and strict residency controls which Redwood supports via Private and Dedicated modes.
- Key blockers: final pricing for dedicated pools, SOC2 docs, and perf traces to validate p95/p99.
- Follow-ups: send docs, schedule SE deep-dive, draft SOW.
